slides.headline: October 28, 1627: a Mughal emperor died travelling home from Kashmir - leaving behind an empire run partly by his wife.
Emperor Jahangir, Akbar's son, died on October 28, 1627 while travelling back toward Lahore from Kashmir
slides.body: He had ruled the Mughal Empire since 1605, consolidating its administration while presiding over what's considered the golden age of Mughal painting.

slides.eyebrow: A marriage that shaped an empire
slides.headline: His wife, Nur Jahan, wielded major political influence throughout his reign - unusually direct power for a Mughal empress.
slides.body: Jahangir also left behind his own memoir, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, giving historians a rare first-person account of Mughal court life, politics and his own reflections, in his own words.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: A Viksit Bharat inherits a four-century-old tradition of written self-record, from courts that understood history needed documenting.
slides.body: Jahangir's own memoir is part of why Mughal-era India is one of history's best-documented empires - a record-keeping instinct modern India's institutions still carry forward.
